Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Thanh Nguyen is a 31-year-old Vietnamese American carpenter, married, who presented for his initial intake following a traumatic encounter with police approximately fourteen months ago. He described the incident in measured but strained terms: he had been pulled over late one evening while driving home from a job site, still wearing his work clothes and with tools visible in the back of his truck. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated rapidly when a second patrol car arrived. Thanh was ordered out of the vehicle, and within moments he found himself face-down on the asphalt with an officer's knee pressed into his back, his arms wrenched behind him, and a second officer standing over him with a weapon drawn. He remained pinned to the ground for what he estimates was close to ten minutes, unable to move, unable to explain himself, with his face turned sideways against the cold road and the flashing blue and red lights strobing above him. He was eventually released without charge. No explanation was offered.

In the weeks that followed, Thanh found himself returning to the night again and again, not by choice but compulsively, the way a tongue finds a broken tooth. He would replay the sequence of events while cutting timber at work, while eating dinner with his wife, while lying in the dark unable to sleep. Each replay carried the same destination: the conclusion that he had done something to bring it on himself, that he had been too slow to comply, that he should have spoken differently, moved differently, been different. He had come to hold this belief with a quiet but absolute conviction, and it sat in him like a splinter he could not locate. Alongside this, he began using marijuana daily, initially to blunt the edges of evenings that felt too exposed, too uncontrolled.

The physical dimensions of his distress took on a particular shape at work. Thanh spends most of his days in clients' homes and renovation sites - open spaces, unfamiliar rooms, doorways at his back. He had gradually, without fully articulating it to himself, reorganized how he moved through these spaces. He now positions himself whenever possible with his back against a wall or a solid surface, facing the room, watching the entry points. On a recent kitchen remodel, his foreman commented that Thanh kept drifting away from the work area to stand near the far wall. Thanh said nothing, but the observation embarrassed him. He was certain that something bad could arrive at any moment from a direction he wasn't watching, and the only reasonable response was to never stop watching.

This vigilance extended beyond physical space. When a materials delivery ran late on a job site, Thanh's mind moved immediately to catastrophe - an accident, something wrong, a situation already beyond recovery. He could not locate the logic of this in the delay itself, but the feeling was not open to argument. Similarly, even in moments that were objectively quiet - evenings at home, weekends with his wife - he could not settle. Relaxation felt not like rest but like exposure, like the moment before something he couldn't see arrived. His wife, Linh, had noticed the change in him over the months. He had become quieter, more watchful, and when she asked what was wrong, he changed the subject. He had not told her the full details of what happened that night, partly because he did not want to revisit it and partly because he had come to feel, in some way he could not entirely articulate, that it reflected something about him that he did not want her to see.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a conversation with his brother, who had noticed how much weight he had lost and how rarely he smiled. Thanh made the appointment the following week. He arrived early, took the chair nearest the wall, and spent the first several minutes of the session scanning the office. What he said he most hoped for was to stop feeling like he was always waiting for something terrible to happen. What he was most afraid of, he admitted quietly, was that the person he had become since that night might be the person he was going to stay.
